extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or evaluating short moral/literary essays for a periodical (The Spectator-style), including use of anecdote, fable, satire, and moral commentary aimed at a general educated public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity of Conquests / Criteria for judging conquests
rubrics_metrics.description: A conquest is truly profitable only if it renders the conqueror master of more subjects, more riches, or greater power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set gains against losses: count newly acquired subjects, but subtract lives lost in war (estimates given: e.g. armies of ~200,000 in the field; 40,000 yearly casualties leading over decades to hundreds of thousands lost), famine mortality, banishments, and long-term demographic effects (reduced births, emigration). Also consider economic effects: loss of industry, insecurity of property, diminished revenue. Use concrete arithmetic and historical analogies (Pyrrhus) to show when victory becomes ruinous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate a ruler at his apparent height (but still weigh ambition)
rubrics_metrics.description: When drawing a portrait of a great conqueror, it is reasonable to consider him at the time of his greatest success (example: at the Peace of Ryswick), but even then ambition may be judged vain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the state at the conqueror's zenith with later reverses; showing that even at peak the costs and hollow nature of gains can be evident strengthens the critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable: primary purpose — instruct without offending
rubrics_metrics.description: A good fable conveys instruction and moral truth, and is particularly valuable when it can address or correct powerful persons without giving offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fables have durability across ages and manners (Jotham, Nathan, Aesop). They are effective because they teach by allegory and can reach rulers and mobs more safely than direct admonition. Use clear, simple moral lessons and aim for persuasiveness rather than mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable: choice of mode — beasts/vegetables or personified passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fables may use brutes and plants as actors, or may allegorize using passions, virtues, and vices as dramatis personae; both modes have advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select animals/vegetables when you need accessible, universal exempla; select personified passions (as in allegorical epics) when you wish to represent internal human conflicts (examples: Homer interpreted allegorically; Spencer's Fairy-Queen; Prodicus' Hercules choosing Pleasure/ Virtue). Match mode to intended audience and moral subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable as vehicle for philosophical or political instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Fables can encapsulate philosophical observations (e.g., the inseparability of pleasure and pain) and political counsel in an engaging, memorable form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personification and a compact narrative to embody an abstract truth (example given: Pleasure and Pain marriage allegory). Tie the moral to everyday experience so readers readily see the lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental forgiveness as a moral duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents who refuse to forgive children who have married without consent or otherwise erred show unnatural hardness of heart; compassion and forgiveness are duties rooted in natural instinct and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue from human instinct (dependence creates a perpetual claim on tenderness), from reciprocity (we ask forgiveness from God only if we forgive others), and from prudence. Use moving, natural anecdotes (e.g., Eginhart/Imma story) to persuade an obdurate parent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to the practice of 'insnaring' women (seduction and abandonment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of luring young women into sexual relations and abandoning them ('insnaring') is a social wrong that should be treated as seriously as property theft or robbery of honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose and stigmatize the practice publicly so it is as infamous as stealing clothes; use legal remedies where possible (warrants, evidence), and employ practical measures (decoy/entrapment by injured parties) to secure prosecution. Advocate social sanctions that make seducers dread the imputation of their acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anecdote, mock-advertisement, and reportage for satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical essays can use the forms of news, advertisement, or journal entries (mock advertisements, 'historiographer' journals) to lampoon social types and habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a plausible factual frame (dates, small details, daily progression) to give the satire verisimilitude (example: the journal of 'Nicholas Hart' who sleeps yearly). The restrained, 'reporting' tone heightens the humour and moral point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer touches of nature (pathos, human feeling) over mere wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters or essays that show natural feeling (touches of nature) are more pleasing and persuasive than those that display mere cleverness or wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select submissions and examples that move readers emotionally and represent everyday human tenderness; favour sincerity and pathos when instructing the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a writer discovers a fruitful comic vein, pursue related topics
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line of humour (a 'vein') proves productive, follow it into adjacent themes (e.g., grinning → whistling → yawning → sleeping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow correspondents and follow-up papers to develop the idea; use linked short pieces to expand a comic or moral concept across several instalments for cumulative effect.
